status: prespecified public-data diagnostic; no benchmark executed by Thomas or the assistant
question: Does a matched cloud product price or core count by itself establish the cheapest completed workload, and can public measurements supply a more specific countercheck?
selection: AWS general-purpose 16-vCPU, 64-GiB products using recent Intel, AMD and Arm architectures; a purchasable-cloud-product comparison, not equal physical cores or isolated CPU causality.
outcome_selection: Include every common valid workload/configuration in these two task outputs. Do not choose only favorable tests. Report measured server-plus-client throughput and paired latency, not extrapolated server-only performance. No universal winner or cross-workload composite will be called production economics.
matching_gates: Inspect CPU model, threads per core, memory and virtualization before interpretation.
Require matching task hash and software version for each task; architecture-specific binary builds may differ and must be disclosed.
Compare common payload, pipeline and concurrency settings; retain all common settings.
If pricing is added, use the same region, OS, tenancy and on-demand term and disclose pricing date separately from benchmark date.
No synthetic score is allowed to infer Intel realized ASP, shipment share or segment margin.
known_limits_before_scores: These are noncontemporaneous archival observations, not a randomized simultaneous experiment.
One saved machine variant per instance; no independent-machine sampling confidence interval.
Client and server share the same instance; CPU scheduling is part of the observed product result.
PostgreSQL excluded because matched observations are not present in all three selected instances.
Arm kernel is disclosed; older x86 metadata lacks that field, so software environment is incompletely matched.
